title: Lecture 2: Why EAs: optimisation and hardness
outline:
VIDEO: 'Lecture 2: Why EAs: optimisation and hardness' (Nature-Inspired Computation, ECM3412). Ten scenes, 108 s, square 1080 x 1080, no narration. The story is told problem-first (the app's guidebook has the generic EA first; the video ends on it as the pay-off to the title 'Why EAs?'): 1 title (4 s); 2 fitness: bits, f(s) and exhaustive search on the 3-item problem (12 s); 3 the catch: every extra item doubles the solutions, then the New York Tunnels numbers (12 s); 4 polynomial vs exponential: curves that cross, then real seconds (11 s); 5 an easy problem: Prim on the 5-town MST (12 s); 6 its hard cousin: the degree rule makes greedy fail, 20 vs 19 (12 s); 7 approximate algorithms: nearest-neighbour vs an EA race on a 25-city TSP (13 s); 8 the EA loop: select and vary on the 10-solution population (11 s); 9 update: three rules, the best can be lost (12 s); 10 recap (9 s). Selection pressure / greediness and replacement details are NOT in this video on purpose (Lecture 4's video covers them); keep scene 8 and 9 light on those.

LECTURE FACTS EVERY SCENE RELIES ON (all numbers below were computed in node and must be reproduced by code, never typed):
OPTIMISATION (2.2): items 20 kg, 75 kg, 60 kg, target 100 kg. A solution = 3 bits, 1 = take the item (first bit = item 1). Search space S = 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 solutions. Fitness f(s) = |weight - 100|, smaller is better (minimisation). Table (bits, weight, f): 000 0 100 | 001 60 40 | 010 75 25 | 011 135 35 | 100 20 80 | 101 80 20 | 110 95 5 | 111 155 55. Best = 110, f = 5. Trying all 8 and keeping the best = exhaustive search (enumeration): guaranteed optimal but only possible when S is small. n items give 2^n subsets: 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 (about 1 billion). Real fitness functions (not drawn): timetabling = number of clashes (minimise), car design = distance on terrain (maximise).
COMPLEXITY (2.3): easy (tractable) = a polynomial-time exact algorithm is known (sorting n log n, minimum spanning tree). Hard (intractable) = the fastest known exact algorithm is exponential (2^n, 1.1^n; TSP by trying every tour is n!, timetabling). Hard does not mean a big search space (sorting has n! orderings but is easy). An exponential always overtakes a polynomial: 1.1^n vs n^1.1: n=10 2.59 vs 12.59; n=20 6.73 vs 26.99; n=43 60.24 vs 62.63; n=44 66.26 vs 64.24 (they cross between 43 and 44); n=50 117.39 vs 73.94; n=60 304.48 vs 90.36. Real time at 10^9 steps per second and n = 60: n^2 = 3,600 steps = 3.6 microseconds; 2^60 = 1.15 x 10^18 steps = 1.15 x 10^9 s = 36.5 years (31,557,600 s per year); n! for n = 60 is far longer than the age of the universe.
MST (2.4): 5 towns A-E, 10 possible cables with costs AB 12, AC 4, AD 6, AE 9, BC 7, BD 8, BE 3, CD 5, CE 6, DE 14. A spanning tree connects every town with no cycle and has exactly n - 1 = 4 edges. Prim (greedy), starting at A, each step adds the cheapest edge joining the tree to a NEW town: candidates {AB12 AC4 AD6 AE9} -> AC 4; {AB12 AD6 AE9 BC7 CD5 CE6} -> CD 5; {AB12 AE9 BC7 BD8 CE6 DE14} -> CE 6; {AB12 BC7 BD8 BE3} -> BE 3; total 4 + 5 + 6 + 3 = 18 = the optimum (polynomial time, guaranteed optimal: an EASY problem). Its edges give degrees A1 B1 C3 D1 E2. Add the real-world rule 'no town may have more than 2 cables' (degree <= 2): the optimum (C has 3) is now infeasible; greedy Prim that skips infeasible edges: AC 4 (A1 C1); CD 5 (C2 = full, D1); candidates AB12 AE9 BC7 BD8 CE6 DE14 with BC and CE blocked because C is full -> BD 8 (B1 D2 = full); candidates AE9 BE3 CE6 DE14 with CE and DE blocked -> BE 3; total 4 + 5 + 8 + 3 = 20. Brute force over all 125 spanning trees: the best tree with every degree <= 2 is the path D-A-C-E-B = AD 6 + AC 4 + CE 6 + BE 3 = 19 (the only one costing 19; 60 trees satisfy the rule). So greedy gets 20 but 19 exists: greedy never looks ahead, and the constrained problem has no known fast exact algorithm: HARD. Lecture trees for reference: AB DE BC BE = 36, AC AD BC BE = 20.
APPROXIMATE (2.5): an exact algorithm guarantees an optimum; for hard problems that means basically exhaustive search, far too slow. New York Tunnels (simplified water network): 21 pipes, 16 possible diameters each, 16^21 = 19,342,813,113,834,066,795,298,816 = 1.9 x 10^25 designs; at 10^9 designs per second = 1.93 x 10^16 s = 6.13 x 10^8 years (the lesson says about 600 million years). Approximate algorithms: reasonable time, pretty good (often optimal) solutions, but NO guarantee of optimality (sat-nav analogy). Quality-vs-time curve: a simple method is good fast but levels off; a sophisticated method (an EA) is slow but better eventually. The lecture's live race: 25-city TSP, nearest neighbour vs a steady-state EA (population 30, tournament of 3, segment-reversal mutation, child replaces the worst if no worse). With the seeded instance in helpers (seed 16): nearest neighbour = 4.314 instantly; the EA's best tour length is 9.065 after 30 evaluations, 8.403 @100, 5.836 @300, 4.987 @1000, crosses below the nearest-neighbour length at evaluation 1949 (4.116), 3.756 @3000 and 3.563 from evaluation 3801 on, which is 17.4 % shorter than nearest neighbour (its tour has no self-crossing). EAs are approximate algorithms, among the most successful and general.
GENERIC EA (2.1): a population P of random solutions (typically 100-500) each with a fitness, then repeat Select (choose parents, biased to fitter but not only the best) -> Vary (genetic operators: mutation, recombination; children can be better OR worse) -> Update the population. The lecture's population of 10 (fitness, higher is better): S1 0.1, S2 0.5, S3 0.3, S4 0.2, S5 0.9, S6 0.7, S7 0.3, S8 0.4, S9 0.4, S10 0.1 (mean 0.39). Parents S5 (0.9) and S9 (0.4). Children S11 = 1.0 (better) and S12 = 0.2 (worse). Update rules: 1) replace the entire population with children (S5 is LOST); 2) merge old + new (12) and keep the best 10: sorted S11 1.0, S5 0.9, S6 0.7, S2 0.5, S8 0.4, S9 0.4, S3 0.3, S7 0.3, S4 0.2, S12 0.2 | S1 0.1, S10 0.1 -> S1 and S10 drop out, mean 0.49; 3) replace some old with some new, e.g. the weakest: S1 and S10 (0.1) are replaced by S11 and S12, same survivors, mean 0.49. Rules 2 and 3 never lose the best. NOTE for the team: the app text of module 2.1 (js/content/nic/l12-03.js, merge note) says S12 does not get in; that is wrong (S12 ties S4 at 0.2 and survives; only S1 and S10 drop). The video follows the computation.
COLOUR ROLES IN THIS VIDEO (consistent in every scene): green = good / valid / best / optimal / easy / kept / the 100 kg target; red = bad / hard / lost / blocked / the gap f and the 'exponential'; blue = the items and solutions we look at, the start town; orange = chosen things (selected parents, candidate cables, the new half in the doubling grid) and the nearest-neighbour method; purple = operators and their output (the formula tag, 'vary', children, the dice); grey = neutral (the population, the shelf, plain tags). The EA loop strip is orange (Select), purple (Vary), green (Update) in scenes 8, 9 and the recap. Numbers and labels >= 28 px, everything inside the stage with >= 12 px margin, UK spelling, no white, symbols drawn as SVG.

titleCard.sub: Optimisation, hardness and the generic EA

title: Every solution gets
a fitness score
scenes.spec:
IDEA: a solution is a bit string, a fitness function scores it, and trying all 8 (exhaustive search) finds the best. Reuse L5.chromosome (bit tiles), L2.subsets, L2.star.
DATA (all computed in code by L2.subsets(): items 20 / 75 / 60 kg, target 100, f = |weight - 100|, bit 1 = take the item, first bit = item 1): 000 w0 f100 | 001 w60 f40 | 010 w75 f25 | 011 w135 f35 | 100 w20 f80 | 101 w80 f20 | 110 w95 f5 | 111 w155 f55. Best = 110, f = 5.
LAYOUT (ruler: 5.2 px per kg from x 60, so 100 kg sits at x 580): (a) SHELF y 0-64: three blue sticker blocks at x 60 / 184 / 594 with widths 104 / 390 / 312 (20 / 75 / 60 kg) and the labels '20 kg', '75 kg', '60 kg' (28 px) inside. (b) BIT TILES (three one-tile L5.chromosome rows, or one row moved per tile with row.set(i, {x}); size 52, each tile centred under its shelf block, y 72-124): 1 = solid blue tile, 0 = grey ghost tile. (c) STACK ROW y 150-214: the taken blocks sit end to end from x 60 with the same widths, so the stack length is weight x 5.2; a block that has left the shelf leaves a dashed placeholder there. (d) TARGET: a green dashed vertical line at x 580 from y 136 to 282, drawn behind the blocks, with a solid green tag '100 kg' centred at (580, 112). (e) GAP BAR y 226-238: a red rounded 12 px bar from the end of the stack to x 580 (left of the line when under 100, right of it when over) with a red tag 'f = N' centred under it (y 244-288). (f) FORMULA: a purple tag 'f(s) = |weight − 100|' centred at (468, 318). (g) THE SEARCH SPACE: 8 cards, y 356-632, each 98 wide, gap 12, from x 34. Card = bit string at the top (v-mono, 32 px), a red bar standing on the card floor (44 wide, height = f x 1.5 px so f = 100 is 150 px) and its f value (30 px bold) just above the bar. An untried card is grey and dashed with the bit string only.
TIMELINE (local s): 0.2-1.4 the shelf blocks pop in one by one (stagger 0.2). 0.8-1.4 the target line draws downwards and its tag pops. 1.6-2.4 the formula tag and the 8 empty cards pop in (stagger 0.06). TRIALS: trial k = 0..7 in binary order (000, 001, ... 111) runs from 2.8 + 0.85k to 3.65 + 0.85k: the tiles flip (0-0.2), the previous trial's blocks fly back to the shelf while this trial's taken blocks fly from the shelf down to the stack (0.1-0.45, ease inOut), the gap bar grows and its f tag pops (0.4-0.65), card k's bar pops up (ease.pop) and its value appears (0.6-0.85). Trial 000 shows an empty stack and a 520 px gap bar (f = 100). 9.8-10.6: the other 7 cards dim to 50 %, card 110 turns green (border, bar), an orange star pops on it, and the stack re-forms 110 (items 1 and 2 = 95 kg) with a green 5 kg gap bar and the tag 'f = 5' (green). Hold to the end.
CAPTIONS: [0.3, 2.4, "Three items. Aim for 100 kg in total."], [2.6, 4.8, "Bits: 1 takes an item, 0 leaves it."], [5.0, 7.8, "Fitness f(s): how far from 100 kg. Smaller is better."], [8.0, 9.7, "Exhaustive search: try every subset."], [9.9, 11.5, "Try all 8: 110 is the best."].
FINAL STATE: the 8 filled cards with 110 green and starred, the other 7 dimmed, the shelf with items 1 and 2 shown as dashed placeholders, the 95 kg stack with the green 5 kg gap, the target line. Scene 3 starts from 'there are 8 solutions'.

title: Every extra item
doubles the work
scenes.spec:
IDEA: every extra item doubles the number of solutions, so trying them all stops being possible; a real design problem is astronomically bigger. Reuse L2.fmt, L2.sci, L2.hash, L2.clock.
DATA: 2^3 = 8, 2^4 = 16, 2^5 = 32, 2^6 = 64; 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 (about 1 billion). New York Tunnels (simplified water network): 21 pipes, 16 diameters each; designs = 16^21 = 19,342,813,113,834,066,795,298,816 = 1.9 x 10^25 (compute with BigInt, show '1.9 × 10²⁵'); at 10^9 designs per second that is 1.934e16 s = 6.13 x 10^8 years (31,557,600 s per year), shown as 'about 600 million years' as in the lesson.
PHASE A, 0-5.9 (the doubling grid): cells are 40 px squares, gap 6, blue soft stickers (the 8 solutions of scene 2). The grid starts as 4 columns x 2 rows at the left (top-left (60, 150)). Doubling steps: a copy slides in BELOW (4 x 4 = 16), then to the RIGHT (4 rows x 8 cols = 32), then BELOW (8 x 8 = 64, 362 x 362 px); keep the grid vertically centred around y 220 as it grows. The new half is orange while it slides in (0.4 s) and then turns blue; a purple tag '× 2' bobs at the seam. Right column x 500-900: a blue tag '3 items' (then '4 items', '5 items', '6 items') at y 90 and the count as a 120 px number below it ('8', '16', '32', '64') that pops at each step. Timeline: 0.3-1.3 the 8 cells pop in (stagger 0.05) with '3 items' and '8'; doubling steps start at 1.6, 2.8 and 4.0 (copy slides 0.4 s, colours merge 0.2 s, number pops at +0.5). 5.0-5.7 the grid shrinks to 25 % and slides to the top-left; the tag becomes '30 items' and the number counts up to 1,073,741,824 (red, 64 px, ease out, 5.1-5.9) next to a small red tag '≈ 1 billion'. 5.9-6.3 phase A fades out.
PHASE B, 6.3-11.6 (a real problem): blue tag 'New York Tunnels' at (12, 0). Row of 21 circles (the pipes; pitch 40 from x 48, centre y 150, radius = 4 + index, index 0..15 = the 16 diameters) that spin like slot-machine reels from 6.8: at time t pipe i shows size index floor(L2.hash(i, floor(t x 8)) x 16); they freeze at 9.0 on the frame of t = 9.0. Under the row (y 214-258) grey tags '21 pipes' (left) and '16 sizes each' (right). 7.8: grey sticker '16 × 16 × … × 16 (21 times)' at y 280; 8.6 a red sticker '1.9 × 10²⁵ designs' (52 px bold) pops at y 340-410. 9.2-11.4: L2.clock (r 64, red) at (110, 540) with its hand spinning (angle = 720 x (t - 9.2) deg, i.e. 2 turns per second); beside it a grey tag '10⁹ designs a second' (x 210, y 470) and in red 52 px bold '≈ 600 million years' (x 210, y 530).
CAPTIONS: [0.3, 2.4, "3 items make 8 possible solutions."], [2.6, 5.4, "Each extra item doubles the count."], [6.3, 8.5, "A real water network: 21 pipes, 16 sizes each."], [8.7, 11.5, "Trying every design takes 600 million years."].
FINAL STATE: red '1.9 × 10²⁵ designs', the stopped pipes, the clock and '≈ 600 million years'. Scene 4 starts a fresh figure (the plot).

title: An exponential always
wins in the end
scenes.spec:
IDEA: even a tiny exponential overtakes a polynomial as n grows, and in real time the difference is microseconds against years (easy vs hard). Reuse L6.plot (curves + points), L2.sup, L2.fmt, L5.arrow.
DATA (Math.pow in code): 1.1^n vs n^1.1: n=10 2.59 vs 12.59; n=20 6.73 vs 26.99; n=43 60.24 vs 62.63; n=44 66.26 vs 64.24 (cross between 43 and 44, the crossing point is about (43.5, 63.4)); n=60 304.48 vs 90.36. Phase 2 at n = 60, 10^9 steps per second: n^2 = 3,600 steps = 3.6 µs; 2^60 steps = 1.15 x 10^9 s = 36.5 years.
PHASE 1 LAYOUT: L6.plot at (12, 0), w 912, h 470, xmin 0, xmax 60, ymin 0, ymax 320, xticks [0, 20, 40, 60], yticks [0, 100, 200, 300]. Curves w 8: polynomial n^1.1 in green, exponential 1.1^n in red, each with a dot at its front (r 10). Name tags in the empty upper-left of the plot: green soft tag 'polynomial' and red soft tag 'exponential' (28 px), each a short leader line away from the curves. READOUT ROW y 496-548, centred: grey tag 'n = 20', red tag '1.1ⁿ = 6.7' and green tag 'n¹·¹ = 27.0' (L2.sup; the numbers are the real values at n = floor(cursor), one decimal; use two decimals only if the one-decimal numbers are equal).
PHASE 1 TIMELINE: 0.2-0.9 plot card, axes and tags pop in. 0.9-6.2 a cursor n sweeps piecewise-linearly: n = 2 at 0.9, 30 at 2.7, 44 at 4.4, 50 at 5.3, 60 at 6.2 (slow where it matters). The curves are drawn left to right up to the cursor (k = n / 60) and the readout follows it. The red curve starts below the green one (red 2.6 vs green 12.6 at n = 10); when the cursor passes n = 43.5 (t about 4.3) the crossing dot flashes (ring pulse, V.flash) and a red solid tag 'exponential wins' pops in the empty area above-left of the crossing with a short leader to the dot. 6.5-6.9 the plot, tags and readout fade out.
PHASE 2 (7.0-10.4): a grey tag 'n = 60 · 10⁹ steps a second' at the top-left (12, 0). Two bars stand on a baseline y 470: green bar x 220-370 for 'n²' and red bar x 560-710 for '2ⁿ' (label 44 px under the baseline, y 486, via L2.sup). The green bar is only 8 px tall and a green tag '3.6 µs' sits above it (centred x 295, y 414). The red bar grows 7.6-9.2 (ease in) from 0 up to y 60 (410 px) and leaves the stage through a zig-zag break mark at y 140 with a red up arrow (L5.arrow) above it; a red solid tag '36 years' pops at (635, 12) at 9.2. Below, at y 548: green solid tag 'easy' under the green bar and red solid tag 'hard' under the red bar (pop at 9.6). A small grey tag 'not to scale' at the bottom right (y 600).
CAPTIONS: [0.4, 3.0, "A tiny exponential against a polynomial."], [3.2, 6.2, "At n = 44 the exponential overtakes."], [7.2, 10.5, "At n = 60: microseconds, or 36 years."].
FINAL STATE: the two bars (tiny green, red off the top), tags 3.6 µs, 36 years, easy and hard. Scene 5 opens on the graph of 5 towns.

title: Prim: always take the
cheapest new cable
scenes.spec:
IDEA: the minimum spanning tree is EASY: Prim's greedy algorithm, one cheapest new cable at a time, is fast and always optimal. Reuse L2.graph, L2.prim, L5.badge-style tags (v-tag), V.flash.
DATA: L2.G (5 towns, 10 cables, weights AB 12, AC 4, AD 6, AE 9, BC 7, BD 8, BE 3, CD 5, CE 6, DE 14) and L2.prim(0) run from A. Steps (candidates -> pick -> running total): 1) AB12 AC4 AD6 AE9 -> AC 4 -> 4; 2) AB12 AD6 AE9 BC7 CD5 CE6 -> CD 5 -> 9; 3) AB12 AE9 BC7 BD8 CE6 DE14 -> CE 6 -> 15; 4) AB12 BC7 BD8 BE3 -> BE 3 -> 18. Final tree AC, CD, CE, BE = 18 (4 cables for 5 towns, no loop).
LAYOUT: L2.graph at (0, 24): towns are 68 px circles with letters (36 px) at A (60, 258), B (330, 40), C (285, 467), D (615, 439), E (630, 97) (graph-local, add the offset), every cable a thin grey line (4 px) with its weight in a small grey pill (28 px bold) at the middle of the edge (BD at 0.4 and CE at 0.7 along the edge so those two pills do not collide). Right panel: a plain v-card 'cost' at (700, 40), 224 x 170 (right edge 924): grey 'cost' label on top and the running total in 96 px bold. Bottom: space for one tag at (468 centred, y 570).
TIMELINE (local s): 0.2-1.8 the graph builds: towns pop (A to E, stagger 0.12), cables draw (stagger 0.05), weight pills pop; the cost card pops at 1.4 showing 0. 2.0 town A gets a blue ring (the start). PRIM STEPS: step i = 0..3 starts at 2.2 + 1.7i and lasts 1.7 s: 0-0.5 every candidate cable (edge between a tree town and a non-tree town) turns orange and dashed, its pill orange; 0.5-0.9 the cheapest candidate pulses (scale 1.1, V.flash); 0.9-1.4 it becomes a thick (12 px) solid green line (draw-on from the tree end), the other candidates go back to grey, and the new town gets a green ring; 0.9-1.5 the chosen weight pill flies to the cost card and the total counts up with a pop (4, 9, 15, 18). 9.0-9.6 all four tree cables stay thick green, all five towns green; the cost card turns green with '18'. 9.8 a green solid tag 'easy: fast and optimal' (34 px) pops at the bottom (y 570).
CAPTIONS: [0.3, 2.0, "Connect all 5 towns as cheaply as possible."], [2.2, 5.2, "Prim: take the cheapest cable to a new town."], [5.4, 9.0, "Keep adding the cheapest cable. No loops."], [9.2, 11.6, "Fast and always optimal: an easy problem."].
FINAL STATE: graph with the green tree AC, CD, CE, BE, cost card '18' (green), tag 'easy: fast and optimal'. Scene 6 starts from exactly this picture (same graph, same positions).

title: Add one rule and
greedy gets stuck
scenes.spec:
IDEA: add ONE real-world rule (no town may have more than 2 cables) and the same greedy method fails: it gets 20 while 19 exists. Constrained MST is HARD (no fast exact algorithm known). Reuse L2.graph (same layout as scene 5), L2.prim(2), L2.bestDegree2, L5.cross, L5.arrow.
DATA: L2.prim(2) from A skipping edges that would give a town 3 cables: step 1 AC 4 (total 4; degrees A1 C1); step 2 CD 5 (9; C2 = full, D1); step 3 candidates AB12 AE9 BC7 BD8 CE6 DE14, BC and CE BLOCKED (C is full) -> BD 8 (17; B1 D2 = full); step 4 candidates AE9 BE3 CE6 DE14, CE and DE BLOCKED (D is full for DE, C for CE) -> BE 3 (20). Greedy = AC, CD, BD, BE = 20. The best feasible tree (brute force over all 125 spanning trees, 60 satisfy the rule) is the path D-A-C-E-B = AD 6 + AC 4 + CE 6 + BE 3 = 19.
LAYOUT: the scene 5 graph at (0, 24). Under every town draw two small slot dots (12 px circles, 22 px apart, 46 px below the town centre): one filled dot per cable at that town; a town with 3 cables (C in the optimal tree) gets a red ring and a small red cross (L5.cross) at its top-right. Right panel (x 680-924): an orange v-card 244 x 110 at (680, 0) with two lines 'at most 2' / 'cables per town' (30 px); below it the cost card at (680, 130), 244 x 150, 'cost' label + 96 px number; below it two tags at x 680: red solid 'greedy 20' (y 310) and green solid 'best 19' (y 372). Bottom: a red solid tag 'hard: no fast exact method' (34 px) centred at y 570.
TIMELINE (local s): 0-0.8 the picture of scene 5 is already there (green tree AC, CD, CE, BE, cost 18, no slots yet). 0.8-1.6 the orange rule card pops; the slot dots fade in under the towns and fill (A1, B1, C3, D1, E2); C turns red with the cross and its third dot overflows (flash). 1.9-2.6 the tree edges fade back to thin grey, the dots empty, the cost counts down to 0 and its card turns neutral. GREEDY RUN: step 1 starts 3.0 (1.0 s, same beat as scene 5: candidates orange, cheapest AC pulses and turns thick green, weight flies to the cost card -> 4); step 2 starts 4.0 (1.0 s, CD 5 -> 9, C's two dots fill and C gets an orange ring = full); step 3 starts 5.0 (1.9 s): the candidates turn orange, BC and CE show a red dashed line with a red cross over their pill for 0.9 s (blocked, the pills' weights fade), then the cheapest feasible BD 8 is chosen (-> 17, D full); step 4 starts 6.9 (1.5 s): AE and BE orange, CE and DE red-crossed, BE 3 chosen (-> 20). 8.4-8.9 the cost card turns red '20' and the tag 'greedy 20' pops. REVEAL (9.0-11.0): the four greedy edges dim to light grey; the path D-A-C-E-B draws edge by edge (AD 6, AC 4, CE 6, EB 3; 0.4 s each from 9.2, thick green); the cost card counts 20 -> 19 and turns green; the tag 'best 19' pops at 10.6; at 10.9 the red tag 'hard: no fast exact method' pops.
CAPTIONS: [0.3, 2.5, "New rule: at most 2 cables per town."], [3.0, 5.4, "Run the same greedy method again."], [5.6, 8.6, "An early cheap choice blocks cheaper ones later."], [9.2, 11.5, "Greedy gets 20, but a tree costing 19 exists."].
FINAL STATE: the green path D-A-C-E-B on the graph, cost card '19' green, tags 'greedy 20' (red), 'best 19' (green) and 'hard: no fast exact method'.

title: A quick method,
or a slow better one
scenes.spec:
IDEA: for hard problems we use approximate algorithms: a quick simple method is good at once, an EA is slow at first but overtakes it given time (the lecture's quality-vs-time curve), with no guarantee of optimality. Reuse L6.plot (curve with a function, dashed curve, toPx), L2.tspRace, L2.tourPanel, L5.arrow.
DATA: L2.tspRace(16) (reference code and expected numbers in the helpers spec): 25 cities, nearest-neighbour tour from city 0 with length 4.314; EA best-so-far length 9.065 @30 evaluations, 8.403 @100, 5.836 @300, 4.987 @1000, 4.116 @1949 (first below 4.314), 3.756 @3000, 3.563 from 3801 to 4000; 44 snapshots of the best tour; the final EA tour is 17.4 % shorter than nearest neighbour (show '17 % shorter'). Evaluations map to time as e(t) = 30 + 3970 x clamp((t - 2.6) / 7.4), so the crossing is at t = 6.18 s.
LAYOUT: two tour panels (L2.tourPanel) at the top, a chart at the bottom. Left panel (x 12, y 0, 440 x 316): orange tag 'Nearest neighbour' in its top-left corner, its length in an orange tag at the top-right ('4.31'). Right panel (x 484, y 0, 440 x 316): green tag 'Evolutionary algorithm' top-left, the running best length in a tag at the top-right (red while it is above the nearest-neighbour length, green after). Both panels show the same 25 city dots (r 8, dark ink) mapped as px = panelX + 20 + cx x 400, py = panelY + 56 + cy x 240, and one closed route (line 5 px): orange on the left, green on the right. Chart: L6.plot at (12, 340), w 912, h 270, xmin 0, xmax 4000, no ticks; plot quality UP: y value = -tourLength, ymin -9.4, ymax -3.4, so a shorter tour is higher. A small grey tag 'time' bottom-right inside the chart and a grey tag 'better' with a small up arrow (L5.arrow) top-left inside it. Nearest neighbour = a dashed orange horizontal line at -4.314 (L6.plot curve with dash); the EA = a solid green curve of -best(e) drawn up to the playhead, with a dot at its front.
TIMELINE (local s): 0.2-0.8 both panels and the chart card pop in, city dots pop (stagger 0.02). 0.8-2.4 the nearest-neighbour route draws city by city in orange (the order from L2.tspRace, closing leg last); 2.4 its length tag pops. 2.0-2.8 the dashed orange line draws across the chart from x = 0 with a small orange tag 'instant' above its right end. 2.6-10.0 the EA runs: e(t) above; the right panel shows the best tour so far (the snapshot with the largest e <= e(t), full route, it jumps at each of the 44 improvements: the first one is a tangle), the length tag counts through the real best values, the green curve extends and its dot follows. At t = 6.18 (evaluation 1949) the curve passes above the dashed line: the length tag flips red to green, the crossing dot flashes (V.flash ring) and a green solid tag 'EA ahead' pops on the chart just above the crossing point. 10.2-10.8 both routes are final, both tags stay ('4.31' orange, '3.56' green) and a green solid tag '17 % shorter' pops at the bottom of the right panel (y 268-308).
CAPTIONS: [0.4, 2.4, "Nearest neighbour: an instant, decent tour."], [2.8, 6.0, "The EA starts from random tangles."], [6.2, 9.8, "Given time, it overtakes the quick method."], [10.2, 12.6, "Approximate: good answers, no guarantee."].
FINAL STATE: left, the orange nearest-neighbour tour (with one self-crossing); right, the tidy green EA tour (no crossings); chart with the dashed orange line below the finished green curve; tags 4.31, 3.56 and '17 % shorter'.

title: Select parents,
then vary them
scenes.spec:
IDEA: an EA keeps a population of solutions, each with a fitness, and repeats Select -> Vary -> Update; this scene shows the first two steps. Reuse L2.bars, L2.loopStrip, L5.arrow (curved, bow), L5.dice, V.flash.
DATA: L2.POP = S1 0.1, S2 0.5, S3 0.3, S4 0.2, S5 0.9, S6 0.7, S7 0.3, S8 0.4, S9 0.4, S10 0.1 (bars; mean 0.39). Parents S5 (0.9, the best) and S9 (0.4, only average): selection is biased towards the fit, not 'best only'. Children L2.KIDS = S11 1.0 (better than both parents) and S12 0.2 (worse than both).
LAYOUT: L2.loopStrip at (48, 0), w 840 (three stickers 'Select' orange, 'Vary' purple, 'Update' green, return arrow underneath, 96 px tall in all). L2.bars with 12 slots, slot s centre x = 60 + 72 s, bar 60 wide, baseline y 548, height = fitness x 320 px (S11 = 320 px, S1 = 32 px), value label (28 px, one decimal) above each bar, name label (28 px) under the baseline. S1..S10 sit in slots 0..9 (grey, soft look); S11 and S12 will appear in slots 10 and 11 (purple, solid). The dice point J = (816, 128) is the join point above the children.
TIMELINE (local s): 0.2-1.2 the strip pops in (all three grey). 0.4-1.6 the ten bars grow from the baseline left to right (stagger 0.1, ease.pop) and their values fade in. 1.9 the strip's Select sticker lights (orange, pulse). 2.2-3.0 S5 and S9 turn orange solid and lift 20 px with a halo ring (pulse); hold to 4.4. 4.6 the Vary sticker lights (purple, pulse) and Select goes back to grey. 4.8-5.6 two curved purple arrows (L5.arrow with bow, drawOn) run from the top of S5 and from the top of S9 up and over the other bars to J; 5.5 a dice (L5.dice size 44, face = 1 + floor((t - 5.6) x 6) % 6 until 6.2, then face 5) pops at J. 5.9-6.9 the children grow: S11 from 0 to 1.0 in slot 10 and S12 from 0 to 0.2 in slot 11 (purple solid), values counting up; two purple arrows run from the dice down to the tops of the two value labels (the long one to S12 drops straight down at x 852 after leaving the dice). 7.2-8.0 under the names a green up arrow (L5.arrow, 36 px) pops below S11 and a red down arrow below S12 (y 592-628): better / worse than the parents. 8.2-8.8 the parents drop back to their slots (no lift, grey) and the arrows from the parents fade. 8.6 the Update sticker lights (green, pulse) while Vary dims.
CAPTIONS: [0.4, 2.2, "A population: 10 solutions, each with a fitness."], [2.4, 4.6, "Select: fitter ones are more likely, not only the best."], [5.0, 8.4, "Vary: children can be better or worse."], [8.6, 10.6, "Next: who stays?"].
FINAL STATE: grey bars S1..S10 in slots 0-9, purple bars S11 (1.0) and S12 (0.2) in slots 10-11 with their up / down arrows, the strip with Update lit, no rule tag yet. Scene 9 starts from exactly this picture.

title: Update: who stays
in the population?
scenes.spec:
IDEA: the Update step decides who stays, and some rules can throw the best solution away. Three rules are tried on the same twelve solutions. Reuse L2.bars, L2.loopStrip, L2.updateRules, L5.cross, L5.tick, L5.arrow, L5.badge (texts 'best kept' / 'best lost').
DATA (L2.updateRules(), from the lecture's population + children, see the outline): 1) replace everyone: only S11 and S12 remain, S5 (0.9, the best old one) is LOST. 2) merge and keep the best 10: sort order S11 1.0, S5 0.9, S6 0.7, S2 0.5, S8 0.4, S9 0.4, S3 0.3, S7 0.3, S4 0.2, S12 0.2 | S1 0.1, S10 0.1 (cut after the tenth: S1 and S10 drop out, S12 stays), mean 0.49. 3) replace the weakest: the two lowest, S1 and S10 (0.1), are replaced by S11 and S12, mean 0.39 -> 0.49. Rules 2 and 3 keep S5.
LAYOUT: exactly scene 8's end state: L2.loopStrip at (48, 0) with Update lit, L2.bars (12 slots, slot s centre x = 60 + 72 s, baseline y 548, 320 px per 1.0): S1..S10 grey in slots 0-9, S11 and S12 purple in slots 10-11. A rule tag (a v-tag with a small number badge 1 / 2 / 3, 32 px text) centred at (468, 126) names the current rule: 'Replace everyone' (grey), 'Merge, keep the best 10' (orange), 'Replace the weakest' (purple); only one tag is visible at a time (the next one replaces it with a pop). Every rule starts from the same twelve bars, so each phase begins with a 0.3 s cross-fade reset to that state.
RULE 1 (0.7-3.9): 0.7-1.0 the tag pops. 1.1-2.0 the grey bars S1..S10 shrink and fade, left to right (stagger 0.07), except S5: it becomes a red dashed ghost outline (same height) at slot 4 with a red cross (L5.cross, drawOn 1.9-2.3) and its name in red. 1.9-2.6 S11 and S12 slide to slots 0 and 1 (ease inOut). 2.4-2.8 faint dashed grey outlines (56 px tall, no numbers) pop in at slots 2, 3 and 5-9: the other new children, whose fitness is not given. 2.9 a red L5.badge 'best lost' pops above the S5 ghost. Hold, then 3.5-3.9 cross-fade back to the twelve bars.
RULE 2 (4.0-8.1): 4.0-4.3 the tag pops. 4.4-5.4 the twelve bars slide to the sorted slots in the order above (V.ease.inOut, staggered by distance; S11 and S12 keep their purple). 5.5-5.9 an orange dashed vertical cut line draws at x = 60 + 72 x 9.5 = 744 from y 190 to 600. 6.0-6.8 the two bars right of the line (S1 and S10, 0.1) turn red, shrink and fall 60 px, fading. 6.9-7.5 the ten survivors get green outlines, S5 gets a green tick (L5.tick, size 40) over its value and a green L5.badge 'best kept' pops at (468, 168). Hold, then 7.7-8.1 cross-fade back to the twelve bars.
RULE 3 (8.2-11.5): 8.2-8.5 the tag pops. 8.6-9.0 S1 and S10 (the weakest, 0.1) turn red and pulse. 9.0-9.9 S1 and S10 shrink away while S11 slides into slot 0 and S12 into slot 9 (ease inOut). 10.0-10.4 a small grey label 'average' with two tags '0.39' (grey) and '0.49' (green solid) joined by a short L5.arrow pops at (468, 168); S5 carries its green tick. 10.4-11.4 the loop closes: the strip's return arrow draws on (loop 0 -> 1) from Update back to Select and Select pulses (orange).
CAPTIONS: [0.8, 3.4, "Replace everyone: the best can be lost."], [4.2, 7.6, "Merge, keep the best 10: the best survives."], [8.4, 10.0, "Replace the weakest: the best survives too."], [10.2, 11.5, "Then repeat the loop."].
FINAL STATE: the population after rule 3 (S11 in slot 0, S12 in slot 9, S5 ticked), average 0.39 -> 0.49, the strip with the return arrow drawn and Select pulsing.

recap.spec:
Custom bare scene (VID.scene({bare: true, dur: 9, build(stage, V) {...}}), not VID.recapCard, because each point has an animated pictogram), in the style of videos/l6/scene-10-recap.js. Head 'Remember' (v-title-line, 76 px) at (72, 96), Sprout (V.mascot('sprout', {size: 150, mood: 'love'})) at (858, 70). Three sticker cards (v-card plain c-<tone>) at x 72, width 936, height 190, tops 250 / 470 / 690, tones blue, red, green, sliding in (y + 36 -> 0, fade over 0.5 s) at 0.8 / 2.0 / 3.2 s. Each card has a pictogram area 360 x 150 at its left (x + 24, y + 20) and a bold label (v-text big, 44 px, two lines allowed, vertically centred, width 480) starting at x + 420.
ROW 1 (blue) label 'Fitness scores every solution': L5.chromosome of three tiles '1' '1' '0' (size 56, gap 8; the first two blue solid, the third grey ghost) pop in one by one (1.2-1.9); an L5.arrow (grey) draws on 2.0-2.4 to a green solid tag 'f = 5' (28 px) with a small orange star (L2.star) that pops at 2.5-3.0.
ROW 2 (red) label 'Hard problems blow up': a frameless L6.plot (w 330, h 150, x 0 to 10, y 0 to 300; no ticks) at the left of the card; a green curve x² and a red curve 2ˣ draw left to right (k 0 -> 1 over 2.4-3.6, red 0.3 s later); the red curve shoots out of the top of the plot near x = 8.2 (clipped by the plot) while the green one stays low.
ROW 3 (green) label 'EAs: select, vary, update, repeat': three small tiles 1 (orange), 2 (purple), 3 (green) (v-gene size 56, digits) in an arch at (20, 70), (137, 10), (254, 70) with grey L5.arrows 1 -> 2 -> 3 and a curved return arrow under them from 3 back to 1 (these colours and numbers match the loop strip of scenes 8 and 9). They pop in 3.6-4.2; from 4.4 a ring highlight steps through the tiles (tile index = floor(((t - 4.4) % 1.8) / 0.6), the tile pulses with V.flash when lit) and keeps cycling until the end.
BOTTOM: a blue solid tag 'Beat the Lecture 2 boss quiz' (v-tag solid c-blue, 34 px, padding 10 / 28 / 12) centred at x 540, top 925, pops at 5.6-6.1 (scale 0.85 -> 1 with ease.pop, fade in 0.3 s). Hold the finished state until 9.0 (only the row 3 ring keeps cycling). No captions in this scene.

helpers:
HELPER FILES (window.VID.l2, short name L2): videos/l2/common.js (data, algorithms, small utilities, no drawing) and videos/l2/common-2.js (drawing helpers). Create the page videos/lecture-2.html by copying videos/lecture-6.html: title 'Lecture 2 · Why EAs · CSLingo video', same core/motion/cast scripts, then engine.js, cards.js, l5/common.js, l6/common.js, l6/common-2.js, l2/common.js, l2/common-2.js, scene-01-title.js ... scene-10-recap.js, then VID.start. (tools/video-still.js and render-video.js take the page name 'lecture-2'.) Keep every file under 500 code lines (split a scene or a helper file into numbered parts when it nears that); run npx prettier --write and npx eslint on each file. Every draw helper is PURE: it applies exactly the state passed each frame (omitted fields fall back to defaults), keeps no animation state, never uses Math.random, Date, timers or CSS transitions. Positions are stage px (936 x 640), tones are the L5 names green, red, blue, purple, orange, grey. Add assertions at load (throw new Error('lecture 2 data changed')) for the numbers listed under CHECKS.

REUSE FROM VIDEO 5 (VID.l5, videos/l5/common.js): L5.tone(name) gives {c, ink, dim, edge, lip, on} CSS var strings for your own SVG; L5.chromosome(stage, {x, y, genes: '110', size, gap, tone, tones}) (rows of .v-gene tiles with row.set(i, {x, y, s, o, tone, solid, ghost, text}); used for the bit tiles of scene 2 and the recap); L5.arrow(x1, y1, x2, y2, tone, o, {w, head, bow}) with L5.drawOn(g, k) (straight or curved arrows, scene 4, 7, 8, 9, recap; curved parent arcs in scene 8 use bow); L5.tick(x, y, size, tone, opt) and L5.cross(...) (+ drawOn); L5.dice(x, y, size, {face, tone}) (scene 8); L5.badge(stage, {x, y, w, h, valid: 'best kept', invalid: 'best lost'}) (scene 9); L5.svg(stage) a full-stage SVG layer for pictograms. REUSE FROM VIDEO 6 (VID.l6): L6.plot(stage, {x, y, w, h, xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, xticks, yticks, frame}) with plot.curve(fnOrTree, tone, o, {w, dash}) -> c.set({k, o, fn, tone}) (k 0..1 draws left to right, any x => y function works, the curve is clipped to the plot), plot.points, plot.toPx(vx, vy) -> stage px, plot.area; used in scenes 4 and 7 and the recap. Do not use the L6 tree helpers.

common.js (data and algorithms; everything shown on screen is computed here):
- L2.mulberry32(seed) -> () => number in [0, 1) (same function as in js/content/nic/l12-01.js: a |= 0; a = (a + 0x6d2b79f5) | 0; let t = Math.imul(a ^ (a >>> 15), 1 | a); t = (t + Math.imul(t ^ (t >>> 7), 61 | t)) ^ t; return ((t ^ (t >>> 14)) >>> 0) / 4294967296); L2.hash(i, j) -> number in [0, 1) = L2.mulberry32((i + 1) x 7919 + (j + 1) x 104729)() (deterministic 'randomness' for the spinning pipes).
- L2.W = [20, 75, 60]; L2.TARGET = 100; L2.subsets() -> 8 objects {bits: '110', take: [1, 1, 0], w, f} in binary order 000..111 (f = |w - 100|); L2.BEST = '110'.
- L2.POP = [{id: 'S1', f: 0.1}, ... {id: 'S10', f: 0.1}] (0.1, 0.5, 0.3, 0.2, 0.9, 0.7, 0.3, 0.4, 0.4, 0.1); L2.KIDS = [{id: 'S11', f: 1.0}, {id: 'S12', f: 0.2}]; L2.PARENTS = ['S5', 'S9']; L2.mean(list); L2.updateRules() -> {replaceAll: {kept: ['S11', 'S12'], lost: [all ten old ids]}, merge: {order: [12 ids sorted by f desc, stable, ties in S1..S12 order], kept: first 10, dropped: ['S1', 'S10']}, weakest: {replaced: ['S1', 'S10'], kept: [...], meanBefore: 0.39, meanAfter: 0.49}} computed from the data (sort with the stable Array.sort; weakest = the two lowest f, ties by lower index).
- L2.G = {pos: {A: [60, 258], B: [330, 40], C: [285, 467], D: [615, 439], E: [630, 97]} (graph-local px), edges: [['A','B',12], ['A','C',4], ['A','D',6], ['A','E',9], ['B','C',7], ['B','D',8], ['B','E',3], ['C','D',5], ['C','E',6], ['D','E',14]], labelAt: {BD: 0.4, CE: 0.7} (fraction along the edge from the first letter, default 0.5)}; L2.edge(key) -> [a, b, w] for 'AC' style keys (alphabetical).
- L2.prim(maxDeg = 0, start = 'A') -> {steps: [{cands: ['AB12', ...], blocked: [...], pick: 'AC', w: 4, total: 4, deg: {A: 1, ...}}], tree: ['AC', 'CD', 'CE', 'BE'], cost}; maxDeg > 0 skips (and reports as blocked) candidates where either end already has maxDeg cables; stops if no feasible candidate. L2.bruteTrees(maxDeg = 0) -> {count, best: {cost, edges}, feasibleCount} over all 4-edge subsets of the 10 edges that form a tree. L2.bestDegree2 = L2.bruteTrees(2).best (cost 19, edges ['AC', 'AD', 'BE', 'CE']); also expose the path order ['D', 'A', 'C', 'E', 'B'].
- L2.fmt(n) -> '1,073,741,824' (thousands separators); L2.YEAR = 31557600; L2.designs() -> BigInt 16n ** 21n and its mantissa/exponent (1.9342813113834067 x 10^25); L2.sup(base, exp) -> a <span> with the base text and a smaller raised <sup> (use for 1.1ⁿ, n¹·¹, 2ⁿ, 10²⁵ because glyph superscripts may fall back to another font) and L2.sci(mant, exp) -> '1.9 × 10' + sup(25).
- L2.tspRace(seed = 16, N = 25, EV = 4000, P = 30, T = 3) -> {cities, nn, nnLen, best, snaps, crossAt, bestAt(e), tourAt(e), finalLen, finalTour}: copy this code VERBATIM (RNG call order matters; cache the result so it runs once): const r = L2.mulberry32(seed); const ri = (n) => Math.floor(r() * n); cities = Array.from({length: N}, () => [0.05 + r() * 0.9, 0.08 + r() * 0.84]); d(a, b) = Math.hypot of the coordinate differences; len(t) = sum of d(t[i], t[(i + 1) % N]); nn = [0]; left = new Set([1..N-1]); while (left.size) { c = last of nn; b = null; for (const x of left) if (b === null || d(c, x) < d(c, b)) b = x; nn.push(b); left.delete(b); } pop = Array.from({length: P}, () => { a = [0..N-1]; for (let i = N - 1; i > 0; i--) { j = ri(i + 1); [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]; } return a; }); fits = pop.map(len); note(e): bi = fits.indexOf(Math.min(...fits)); best.push(fits[bi]); and when the best length is lower than the last snapshot's (or there is none), snaps.push({e, len: fits[bi], tour: pop[bi].slice()}); call note(P); then for e = P + 1 .. EV: b = ri(P); for (k = 1; k < T; k++) { c = ri(P); if (fits[c] < fits[b]) b = c; } m = pop[b].slice(); i = ri(N); j = ri(N); if (i > j) swap them; m.splice(i, j - i + 1, ...m.slice(i, j + 1).reverse()); fm = len(m); w = 0; for (k = 1; k < P; k++) if (fits[k] > fits[w]) w = k; if (fm <= fits[w]) { pop[w] = m; fits[w] = fm; } note(e). best[e - P] is the best length after e evaluations; nnLen = len(nn); crossAt = P + best.findIndex((l) => l < nnLen); bestAt(e) = best[clamp(e, P, EV) - P]; tourAt(e) = the tour of the last snapshot with snap.e <= e.

CHECKS (assert at load): L2.subsets() best is '110' with f 5 and the f list [100, 40, 25, 35, 80, 20, 5, 55]; 1.1 ** 43 < 43 ** 1.1 and 1.1 ** 44 > 44 ** 1.1; L2.prim(0).tree is ['AC', 'CD', 'CE', 'BE'] with cost 18; L2.prim(2).tree is ['AC', 'CD', 'BD', 'BE'] with cost 20; L2.bruteTrees(0).best.cost 18 over 125 trees; L2.bruteTrees(2).best.cost 19 over 60 feasible trees; 16n ** 21n is 19342813113834066795298816n; L2.updateRules().merge.dropped is ['S1', 'S10'] and its kept list contains 'S12'; L2.tspRace(16): nnLen.toFixed(3) is '4.314', crossAt 1949, finalLen.toFixed(3) '3.563', snaps.length 44, bestAt(30).toFixed(3) '9.065', bestAt(1000).toFixed(3) '4.987'.

common-2.js (drawing; every helper appends its elements to the given parent once and returns an object whose update/set is called every frame):
- L2.bars(stage, {items: [{id, f}] (all 12 up front), x: 24, base: 548, pitch: 72, w: 60, scale: 320}) -> pop with pop.set(id, {slot, dx, dy, s, o, grow, tone, solid, ring, ringTone, dash, value, name, nameTone}) applied immediately: slot = which slot it stands in (default its own index, fractions allowed so bars can slide), dx/dy extra px, s scale about the bar's base centre, o opacity (0 hides everything of that bar), grow 0..1 multiplies the height (the value label shows f x grow with one decimal unless value is false or a string), tone = colour role (default grey soft look; solid: true = saturated sticker fill with -on text for children and picked parents), ring 0..1 = a halo outline in ringTone, dash: true = only a dashed outline (ghost, used for the lost S5 and the placeholders), name = label under the baseline (default the id). Also pop.slotX(slot) -> centre x and pop.topY(id, grow = 1) -> y of the bar top (to place arrows and badges). Bars are .v-card-like stickers (3 px border, 6 px lip), value 28 px bold ink on a tint, name 28 px dim.
- L2.loopStrip(stage, {x: 48, y: 0, w: 840}) -> strip.update({k: 1, active: -1, pulse: 0, loop: 0, o: 1}): three 232 x 64 stickers 'Select' (orange), 'Vary' (purple), 'Update' (green) each with a small number badge 1 / 2 / 3, grey straight arrows between them, and a return arrow drawn underneath from Update back to Select (elbow path, 32 px below the stickers, arrowhead into Select). k 0..1 pops the strip in (staggered), active -1 | 0 | 1 | 2 lights that sticker (saturated, text -on) while the others are grey, pulse 0..1 bumps the active sticker, loop 0..1 draws the return arrow on (in the colour of Select, with draw-on). Total height 96 px.
- L2.graph(stage, {x: 0, y: 24}) -> g.update({k: 1, nodes: {A: {tone, ring: 0..1, ringTone, pulse: 0..1, deg: n, limit: 0 | 2, flash: 0..1}}, edges: {AC: {tone, w, dash, k: 0..1 draw-on from the first letter's town, o, blocked: 0..1, dim: 0..1, pill: tone, pillO}}, o: 1}) and g.pt('A') -> {x, y} centre in stage px, g.pill('BD') -> {x, y} centre of the weight pill, g.r = 34. Towns: 68 px circles with a letter (36 px, 900) (grey sticker by default, the tone when given), edges: 4 px grey lines under the towns by default, with the weight in a pill (28 px bold, panel fill, 3 px border in the edge tone, L2.G.labelAt positions). k 0..1 builds the graph in (towns first, then edges, then pills). An edge in a tone is drawn thick (w default 12) and solid; dash: true gives a dashed edge. blocked 0..1 turns the edge dashed red, fades the weight and pops a red L5-style cross over the pill. When limit is 2 each town shows two slot dots under it (12 px, 22 px apart, 46 px below the centre) with min(deg, limit) filled; deg > limit gives a red ring, a red cross at the top-right and an overflow flash.
- L2.tourPanel(stage, {x, y, w, h, cities, tag, tone}) -> p.update({tour, draw: 1, dots: 1, tone, o, len, lenTone, flash: 0..1}): a plain sticker card with a tag (28 px, the tone) in its top-left, an optional length tag (28 px, two decimals, e.g. '4.31') at the top-right, the city dots (r 8, dark ink; px = x + 20 + cx x 400, py = y + 56 + cy x 240), and the closed route for `tour` (an array of city indices) as a 5 px line in the tone; draw 0..1 draws it city by city (the closing leg last); dots 0..1 pops the dots in; flash pulses the card border. p.pt(i) -> stage px of a city.
- L2.clock(stage, {x, y, r}) -> c.update({angle, o, s, tone}): a round sticker clock (panel fill, 4 px edge in the tone, 12 tick marks, hub dot) with one hand at `angle` degrees (0 = 12 o'clock, clockwise).
- L2.star(x, y, size, tone = 'orange', opt) -> an SVG <g> five-point star sticker (tone fill, lip stroke) to append to your own SVG layer.
- Tags are plain .v-tag elements; build them with V.h('div', {class: 'v-tag solid c-green', style: {...}}, ...children) so L2.sup children work.

Scene-specific drawing stays in the scene files (the item blocks and ruler of scene 2, the doubling grid and pipe reels of scene 3, the bar pair of scene 4, the rule tags of scene 9, the recap pictograms).
